lines.trans: What are you doing out here?

words.gram: used as a question particle: вы что = what, are you...

lines.trans: Would you like me to give you all the details?
Maybe your whole kitchen crew is going to start coming out here?

words.gram: present, 3rd person singular, imperfective; может = may be, perhaps

lines.trans: Of course we are.

words.gloss: we will, are we going to

lines.trans: They will not fix it until the day after tomorrow.
You are not going to come out here anymore.
Give Viktoriya Sergeyevna a pair of gloves.
She wants to fix our restroom all by herself.
Wait, where is he?
Where is he? Are you writing this down?
What, is one hand not enough?
Everyone is assembled.

words.gram: neuter singular, nominative; 'всё равно' = it's all the same
preposition + prepositional; в чём дело = what's going on?

lines.trans: Alright then, until they fix the staff restroom.

words.gram: adverb ('Давайте так' = here's what we'll do)

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I'm here.
There's someone here to see you.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to do, to make', paired with 'сделать'.

examples.trans: What are you doing?
I'm making dinner.
Hi, Arkady Borisovich. What are you doing?

meanings.note: Prefix 'под-' ('under, up to') indicates approaching or supporting from below (stem 'робность'). Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common feminine noun meaning 'detail' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: I don't want to hear these details.
Tell me all the details.

examples.text: Я прошу тебя, не надо! Не хочу слышать эти подробности.
examples.trans: I beg you, don't! I don't want to hear these details.

meanings.note: Prefix 'рас-' ('apart, un-, thoroughly') indicates distribution or intensive action (stem 'сказать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'tell', paired with 'рассказывать'.

examples.trans: Tell that to Stalin.

examples.text: Он же слабый, сразу всё расскажет!
examples.trans: He's weak, after all—he'll tell us everything straight away!

examples.text: Я сегодня же расскажу всё Самсону!
examples.trans: I'll tell Samson everything this very day!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'can, to be able', paired with 'смочь'.

examples.trans: I can't today.
That can't be.

examples.text: Этого не может быть. Это наша история.
examples.trans: That can't be. It's our history.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'here', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: The white one? Give me the keys.

examples.text: Мы сюда зачем прилетели? Я сразу сказал: с ним ничего не получится.
examples.trans: What did we even fly out here for? I said from the start: nothing will come of it with him.
Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'all, whole; everyone, everything', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
As you all know...
Share with everyone.

meanings.note: Entered Russian via Polish 'kuchnia' and Middle High German 'küchen', ultimately from Late Latin 'coquina' (from 'coquere', to cook).

examples.trans: And the kitchen is over there.
We are sitting in the kitchen.

examples.text: Проходите, пожалуйста! Как видите, большой коридор, а там кухня.
examples.trans: Come on in, please! As you can see, a big hall, and the kitchen is over there.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'walks'.

examples.text: Мальчик ходит на костылях. А она ещё и активистка.
examples.trans: The boy walks on crutches. And she's an activist, too.

examples.text: Это она со мной познакомилась! Ходила вокруг меня, как акула.
examples.trans: She was the one who met me! She circled around me like a shark.
She circled around me like a shark.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Of course I'll help.
Yes, of course.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'чинить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to fix, repair', paired with 'чинить'.

examples.trans: Can you fix it?
I will try to fix it myself.
And can the state fix a tank?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: I was only looking.
Just one.
I was only looking!

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'слезавтра').

examples.trans: The day after tomorrow is the festival.

examples.text: Послезавтра вы споёте песню на празднике.
examples.trans: The day after tomorrow you will sing a song at the festival.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

выходить.gloss: to go out, to get out

meanings.en: to go out, to get out
meanings.note: Prefix 'вы-' ('out of') marks outward movement or thorough completion (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to go out, to get out', paired with 'выйти'.

examples.trans: I'm going out in a minute.

examples.text: Ты мне даёшь пятьсот рублей, а я выхожу и покупаю тебе лучшую приставку в мире.
examples.trans: You give me five hundred roubles, and I get out and buy you the best console in the world.

examples.text: Но он же выходит в туалет, на кухню.
examples.trans: But he goes out to the bathroom, to the kitchen.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to give', paired with 'давать'.

examples.trans: Give me just one.
Some water, please.

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'glove' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: A good old glove!
Where is my glove?

examples.text: Чем она плоха? Хорошая старая перчатка!
examples.trans: What's wrong with it? A good old glove!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'she; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: She's a lecturer.
I haven't heard of her.

examples.text: Паша, я больше не хочу о ней слышать. Понял?
examples.trans: Pasha, I don't want to hear about her again. Understood?

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to want', paired with 'захотеть'.

examples.trans: I want coffee.
If you don't want to, suit yourself.
They want to build a shopping centre there.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself, myself, himself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, простите меня, пожалуйста. Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, please forgive me. I don't know myself how it happened.

examples.text: Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: I don't know myself how it happened.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'our, ours', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'toilet' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Where's the toilet?
The toilet is in the corridor.
Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'where', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Where's my toy car?
Where's Dad?

examples.text: А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
examples.trans: Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'he; it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Grab him!
It needs a wash.
Four-eyes! Grab him!

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to write', paired with 'написать'.

examples.trans: Why aren't you writing?
I'm writing a letter.
And why aren't you writing?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'hand; arm' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Give me your hand.
I shake your hand! (a goodbye)
Right, cheers then.

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Two days isn't enough.
We have little time.

examples.text: Подождите! Два дня — это же очень мало.
examples.trans: Hold on! Two days is far too little.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'everything, all; that's it', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Everything's fine.
That's it, bye!

examples.text: Мы просто не хотели вас беспокоить. Всё отменим!
examples.trans: We just didn't want to bother you. We'll cancel it all!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'gathering, assembly; collection' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Я вижу, сегодня все в сборе.
examples.trans: I see everyone is here today.
The assembly is scheduled for the morning.

examples.text: Я вижу, сегодня все в сборе. Ладно, давай, докладывай.
examples.trans: I see everyone is here today. Alright, go ahead, report.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to mean'.

examples.trans: What does this mean?
So you're not coming.
Pasha, what does all this mean?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian expressive spoken interjection meaning 'bye', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Bye, Dad!
Bye, darling!
That's it, bye!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.
This is for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'staff, personnel' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is a delicious lunch for the staff.

examples.text: Сегодня обед для персонала готовит наш огузок.
examples.trans: Today our runt is cooking lunch for the staff.

examples.text: Тогда иди быстрее в раздевалку персонала.
examples.trans: Then go faster to the staff locker room.
